paragraphs.text: VI.A. Communications, Light Signals & Runway Lighting Systems
Introduction
How
Radio Communication & Phraseology 						AI.VI.A.K2, AI.VI.A.R1
Understanding is the single most important thought in pilot-controller communications
If you don’t understand, clarify the instruction
Acknowledge each radio call with your aircraft call sign
Brevity is important but, if necessary, use whatever words will get your message across
Good phraseology enhances safety and is the mark of a professional pilot – Pilot/Controller Glossary
RM: Radio Technique (RM: Communication)
LISTEN and THINK before you transmit
Know what you want to say before you say it
Be alert to the sound/lack of sounds in the receiver
Check your volume, frequency, and make sure the microphone isn’t stuck on transmit
Be sure you are within the performance range of your equipment and the ground station equipment
Radio calls can be broken down into Who, Where, What:
Who you are calling, Who you are, Where you are, What you want
Radio calls at non-towered airports can be broken down into a similar format:
Who you are calling, Who you are, Where you are, What you are doing
ATC Clearances & Instructions

ATC Clearance: Authorization for an aircraft to proceed under specified conditions in controlled airspace - Not authorization to deviate from any rule, regulation, minimum altitude, or conduct be unsafe
Pilot Responsibility when Given a Clearance:
Record the Clearance – Write it down
Readback the Clearance
Always read back:
The “numbers,” or the parts containing altitudes, vectors, or runway assignments (AIM 4-4-7)
Taxi instructions (AIM 4-3-18-9)
Runway assignment, clearance to enter a runway, hold short, line up and wait
Land and hold short operation (LAHSO) clearances (AIM 4-3-11-7)
Read back altitudes, altitude restrictions, vectors in the same sequence as they are given
If uncertain of a clearance, immediately request clarification from ATC (FAR 91.123)
It is the responsibility of the pilot to accept or refuse any clearance issued (AIM 4-4-1(b))
FAR 91.3(a):  The PIC is directly responsible for, and the final authority to, operation of the aircraft
If ATC issues a clearance that deviates from a rule/regulation, or would place the aircraft in jeopardy, it is the pilot’s responsibility to request an amended clearance
If a pilot prefers to follow a different course of action than what is in the clearance, the pilot is expected to inform ATC (you are making a request, not telling the controller what you will do)
RM: Declaring Emergencies (AIM 6-1-2 Emergency Condition) 				AI.VI.A.R2
An emergency can either be a distress or urgency condition
Distress: Threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and requiring immediate assistance
Urgency: Concerned about safety and requiring timely but not immediate assistance
Potential distress condition
Do not hesitate to declare an emergency when faced with distress conditions
Ex: fire, mechanical failure, structural damage
An aircraft is at least in an urgency condition the moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position, fuel endurance, weather, or any other condition that could adversely affect flight safety
This is the time to ask for help
Selection and Use of Appropriate Frequencies 					AI.VI.A.K1
Understanding
Understand the purpose of the different ATC frequencies and when to use them
Preflight Planning
Look up the primary frequencies you plan to use on the flight
ATIS, clearance, ground, tower, & other useful frequencies at departure, arrival, divert airports
Found in the Chart Supplement, Sectional Charts, ForeFlight, Airport Diagram, etc.
In Flight
Thorough preflight planning can prevent this from being an issue – be organized and prepared
In the case a frequency needs to be found in flight, use available resources
Autopilot, ATC, planning documents should be organized and accessible (always fly first!)
Radar Assistance (AIM 4-1-17 & 18) 								AI.VI.A.K7
Requirements & Limitations
Radar equipped ATC facilities provide radar and navigation services to VFR aircraft, provided:
You can communicate with ATC, are within radar coverage, and can be radar identified
RM: Limitations
Based on controller discretion
Guidance information is advisory and responsibility for safe flying remains with the pilot
Cannot determine if flight into IMC will result from their instructions
Services include:
Basic Radar Service – Safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited radar vectoring (workload permitting)
Traffic advisories are issued based on radar targets and referenced in terms of the 12-hour clock
TRSA Service - Radar sequencing and separation for VFR aircraft in a TRSA
Class C Services - Separation between IFR/VFR and sequencing of VFR traffic to the airport
Class B Services - Separation based on IFR, VFR and/or weight and sequencing VFR arrivals
Radar assistance does not relieve the pilot of the responsibility to see and avoid other aircraft
Transponders 											AI.VI.A.K4
Provides aircraft information to Air Traffic Control and other aircraft
Transponder Codes
When using flight following/radar assistance ATC assigns you a unique transponder code
Four numbers from 0-7 (4,096 possible codes)
When combined with radar returns, ATC can see the aircraft on their scope with transponder info
Standard Codes: VFR: 1200; Hijack: 7500; Lost Communication: 7600; Emergency: 7700
Different types/modes of transponders broadcast different information
Mode A: Transmits 4-digit code that identifies an aircraft and its position
Mode C: Mode A + ATC can see the aircraft’s altitude
Mode S: Transmits a variety of information to ATC & other aircraft
Unique ICAO address (assigned to each aircraft), heading, speed, other flight related data
Integral to TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) and ADS-B
Lost Communication 									AI.VI.A.K3, AI.VI.A.K6
ATC Light Gun Signals and their Meaning (AIM 4-3-13)
In the case of a loss of radio communication, the tower can communicate through light signals:
General Information (AIM 6-4-2, AIM 4-3-13)
Squawk 7600 to indicate a loss of two-way radio capability
During daylight, acknowledge transmissions/light signals by moving the ailerons or rudder
At night, acknowledge by blinking the landing or navigation lights
Between sunset and sunrise, to get the attention of the tower turn on a landing light and taxi into a position, clear of the active runway, so that the light is visible to the tower
The landing light should remain on until appropriate signals are received from the tower
Disadvantages of Light Signals (AIM 4-3-13)
Pilots may not be looking at the control tower at the time a signal is directed toward their aircraft
Directions are limited since only approval/disapproval of a pilot’s anticipated actions can be transmitted
Lost Communication Procedures
Airborne Aircraft
Receiver Inoperative - Receiving no audio on tower/ATIS frequencies
Remain outside the airspace until the direction and flow of traffic is determined
Advise tower of the failure, aircraft type, position, altitude, intention to land
Enter the pattern, report position, watch for light gun signals from the tower
Transmitter Inoperative - Receive no response to calls, but can receive calls
Follow the previous procedures
If you can hear ATC, they may ask you to acknowledge their radio calls with an ident
Light gun signals may not be necessary
Make all normal radio calls, just in case
Receiver & Transmitter Inoperative
Remain outside of the airspace until the direction and flow of traffic is determined
Enter the pattern, clearing aggressively, and watch for/acknowledge light gun signals
Trouble Shoot the Situation
Check the connections, equipment, receiver/transmitter, volume, try different frequencies, is there an annunciation showing when you are transmitting (is it working?), etc.
Once on the ground, it is prudent to call the tower and explain the situation
Aircraft on the Ground
Radio malfunctions should be repaired before flight
If this is not possible, call ATC and request VFR departure without two-way radio communication
If radio failure occurs while taxiing, watch for light signals / monitor the tower frequency
Runway Status Lights (RWSL) 								AI.VI.A.K8
Automated system providing indication that it’s unsafe to enter, cross, takeoff, or land on a runway
Installed at several major US airports
Processes information from surveillance systems to turn red warning lights on/off
Used in conjunction with ATC – lights and ATC instructions must agree
Runway Entrance Lights (REL)
In-pavement red lights
Warns aircraft waiting to cross/enter a runway that there is conflicting traffic
Takeoff Hold Lights (THL)
In-pavement red lights
Warns aircraft in the takeoff position that the runway is occupied & takeoff is unsafe
More details: FAA Runway Status Lights
Common Errors 										AI.VI.A.K9
Use of improper frequencies
Improper procedure and phraseology for radio communications
Failure to acknowledge or properly comply with ATC clearances and instructions
Failure to understand or properly comply with ATC light signals and/or RWSL
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

WHAT
Communication between the pilot and different ATC controllers throughout the phases of a flight.
Light gun signals provide a means of communicating with the airplane in case radio communication becomes unavailable.

WHY
Operating in and out of a controlled airport, as well as in a good portion of the airspace system, requires an aircraft to have two-way radio communications.  For this reason, a pilot must be well versed in radio procedures. Radio communications is a critical link in the ATC system and understanding proper com procedures strengthens the link and makes flying safer for everyone.

paragraphs.text: VI.B. Traffic Patterns
Introduction
How
The Pattern
Basics
Controlled Field: The pilot receives a clearance to approach/depart and pertinent pattern information
Uncontrolled Field: It’s up to the pilot to determine traffic direction, and comply with the appropriate rules
Standard Traffic Pattern
Pattern Altitude: Usually 1,000’ AGL
A common altitude is the key factor in minimizing collisions at uncontrolled airports
Chart Supplement will usually specify nonstandard pattern altitudes
Standard Traffic Pattern: Left Turns
Pattern Legs
Upwind: Departure leg, flown parallel and in the same direction as runway heading
Crosswind: Transition from the upwind leg to the downwind leg
Perpendicular to upwind, about ½-1-mile from runway
Downwind: Parallel to the landing runway
Heading is opposite the landing runway, approx. ½-1 mile from the runway
Before landing checks & configuration
Start descent abeam landing point
Turn base 45o from the landing point
Adjust for winds, traffic, tower request, etc.
Stronger wind = closer base leg
Due to decreased groundspeed on final
Base: Perpendicular to the runway
Transition between downwind and final
Ground track should be perpendicular to the centerline
Continue descent, adjusting pitch and power to maintain airspeed and glidepath
Landing configuration, if not already configured
Turn to Final
Lead the turn to be established on the extended centerline of the runway
Turn to final should be no closer than ¼ mile, at the appropriate altitude (3o glide slope)
Final: Final descent of the approach, aligned with the landing runway
Crab into the wind to maintain runway centerline
Adjust pitch and power to maintain airspeed, glidepath, and aim point
Double check the Before Landing Checklist is complete and cleared to land
Maintaining Ground Track (on any leg in the pattern)
Goal is to fly a rectangular pattern regardless of wind direction or speed
Crab into the wind
Visual references are helpful
Upwind: Glance behind to ensure maintaining runway centerline
Crosswind: Use the runway as a reference; note and correct for any drift to or from the runway
Downwind: Intersect a point on the plane with the runway centerline (Ex. fuel cap / rivet line)
Flight Controls
Maintain a consistent crosscheck (90% outside, 10% inside)
Use small, controlled inputs to fly the airplane
Pattern Selection 									AI.VI.B.K2, AI.VI.B.K4
Controlled Field 										AI.VI.B.K1
Generally, ATIS will inform the pilot of the runway(s) in use
The pilot receives a clearance to approach / depart as well as pertinent information about the pattern
ATC will specify pattern entry and departure procedures (Where / how to enter and depart)
During the pattern the controller may make adjustments (speed, legs lengths, turns for spacing, etc.)
Uncontrolled Field 										AI.VI.B.K1
Communication – 2 ways, depending on the airport
FSS (Flight Service Station):  Provides advisories (are not air traffic controllers)
Provide wind info, runway in use, altimeter setting, known traffic, NOTAMs, etc.
Initiate contact approximately 10 miles out with altitude, aircraft type, location
Departing: Transmit tail number, type of flight, destination, services desired, etc.
Self-Announced broadcast on CTAF
Announce your position and intentions on the CTAF frequency
Monitor other aircraft calls on CTAF and coordinate as necessary to avoid hazards
Arriving
Overview
Chart Supplement provides pattern altitude & traffic direction for each runway
Observe other aircraft already in the pattern and conform to the traffic pattern in use
If no other aircraft, use ground indicators and wind direction to determine the runway to use
Check indicators 500’ – 1,000’ above pattern altitude
Always enter the pattern at pattern altitude
Descending into the pattern can be dangerous
Avoids descending onto another aircraft and easier to visually acquire other traffic
Pattern Entries
Downwind Entry: Enter at a 45o to midfield downwind
Midfield Entry (pictured, left)
Cross midfield at least 500’ above pattern altitude
When well clear of the pattern (approximately 2 miles), descend to pattern altitude
Enter level, at pattern altitude, at a 45o angle to the downwind leg, abeam the runway midpoint
Entry while descending creates collision hazards and should be avoided
Another method of entry is a midfield entry from the upwind leg side
Alternate Midfield Entry (pictured, right)
Enter at pattern altitude at midfield crosswind and turn downwind
Should not be used when the pattern is congested
Runway Orientation (RM: Disorientation)						AI.VI.B.R2
Visualize your position in relation to the runway on the heading indicator
Confirm runway number with the heading indicator on all pattern legs
Downwind – reciprocal of runway
Base - 90o off
Final – Same as the runway
Takeoff and/or Departing
Climb out on the upwind leg
Remaining in the pattern: turn crosswind past the end of the runway, within 300’ of pattern alt
If departing, continue straight out, or exit with a 45o turn to the left (or right, for a right pattern)
Monitor the radio for traffic in the local area, and announce your intentions
Clear aggressively (other aircraft may not be using radios)
RM: Pattern Spacing (RM: Collision Hazards)							AI.VI.B.R1
Be aware of other aircraft in the pattern, as well as aircraft entering and exiting the pattern
Listen to radio calls to build a mental image of the traffic around you
At an uncontrolled field, announce your intentions
At a controlled field, follow the controller’s instructions/request permission to make a change
Maintain proper airspeed to blend in with the other traffic
On downwind with another aircraft on final, delay the base turn until abeam/past the other aircraft
Adjust upwind to accommodate aircraft on downwind
The pilot is always responsible for seeing and avoiding whether at a controlled or uncontrolled field
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113) 								AI.VI.B.K3
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging
If aircraft of the same category are converging, the aircraft to the other’s right has the right-of-way
Different Categories Converging (basically, least maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way)
Balloon, glider, and airship have right-of-way over airplanes

Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
To depart or land at an airport we’re going to have to use the traffic pattern, I guess it’s pretty important, huh?
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Traffic Patterns involve the rules and procedures associated with flying a proper traffic pattern at a controlled and uncontrolled airport.
Why

Every flight begins and ends at an airport or other suitable landing area. For that reason, it is essential that the pilot learn the traffic rules, procedures, and pattern layouts that may be in use at various airports.
How:
The Pattern
Controlled - The pilot receives a clearance to approach/depart and pertinent pattern information
Uncontrolled - It’s up to the pilot to determine traffic direction, and comply with the appropriate rules
If familiar with the basic rectangular pattern, approaches/departures will be easy at most airports
Standard Traffic Pattern
The Basics
Pattern Altitude: Usually 1,000’ AGL
A common altitude is the key factor in minimizing collisions at uncontrolled airports
The Chart Supplement will usually specify nonstandard pattern altitudes
Standard Traffic Patterns: Left Turns
All turns are left unless otherwise noted (Chart Supplement, Tower, Airport Markings, etc.)
Turns should not be banked more than 30o
Use rudder to maintain coordination; Do not use rudder to increase the rate of turn, this could result in a cross controlled stall
Pattern Legs
Upwind Leg - The departure leg, flown parallel and in the same direction as runway heading
Crosswind Leg – The transition from the upwind leg to the downwind leg
Perpendicular to the upwind leg (90o turn)
Fly the crosswind leg to provide approximately ½ to 1-mile separation from the runway
Downwind Leg - Parallel to the runway of intended landing
The heading flown is opposite the landing runway
Ex: Landing runway 10, downwind heading is 280o (no wind)
Approximately ½ to 1 mile from the runway
Before landing checks, and configuration (flaps, gear) are normally accomplished downwind
Descent is normally started on the downwind leg when abeam the point of intended touchdown
The downwind leg normally continues to a point 45o off the intended landing point, past the approach end of the runway
The turn to the base leg is started at the end of the downwind leg
Point can be adjusted based on circumstances
Wind, traffic, tower, emergency, etc.
Base Leg - Perpendicular to the runway and the transition between downwind and final
Ground track should be perpendicular to the extended centerline
Heading is 90o off runway direction (with no wind)
Continue the descent, adjusting pitch and power to maintain airspeed, glideslope, aim point
Begin the turn to final to end up established on centerline
Establishing Final Approach
The base leg will be adjusted depending on wind conditions
The stronger the wind, the closer the base leg should be to the runway because of the decreased groundspeed on final
At a slower the groundspeed on final, it takes longer to reach the runway than it otherwise would, and therefore more altitude is lost in the descent
Turn to final should be no closer than ¼ mile at an altitude appropriate for the glide slope selected
A 3o glide slope is normal; a 3o glide slope means we descend 300’ every mile
Final - The final descent of the approach, aligned with the landing runway
Adjust the turn from base to center the aircraft on the runway
Crab into the wind to maintain ground track
Adjust pitch and power as necessary to maintain airspeed, glideslope, and aim point
Run through the Before Landing checklist again to ensure everything is complete, and ensure you have been cleared to land
Departing the Pattern
Climb out on the upwind leg
If remaining in the pattern, turn to the crosswind leg past the departure end of the runway and within 300’ of pattern altitude
If departing, continue straight out, or exit with a 45o turn to the left (or right, for a right pattern)
Maintaining the Desired Ground Track (on any leg in the pattern)
The goal is to fly a rectangular pattern regardless of the wind direction or speed
The airplane will have to be crabbed into the wind to maintain a straight ground track
Maintain awareness of wind in relation to the aircraft, adjust heading as necessary to maintain ground track
Visual references are very helpful in maintaining ground track
Upwind: Glance behind briefly to ensure you are maintaining the runway centerline
Crosswind: Use the runway as a reference; note and correct for any drift to or from the runway
Downwind: Place the runway centerline on a reference point on the airplane
EX: Place the runway centerline on the edge of a stall strip or outside the fuel cap (whatever reference works for your comfort, the aircraft, and the local pattern procedures)
Final: Maintain the centerline, crab as necessary to correct for the wind
Familiar airports may have well known references for the pattern
Ex: Turn base over a field, or road intersection
These are helpful for learning the pattern, but these specific references will not exist at other airports; be sure to teach references that can be carried from airport to airport
Altitude & Airspeed Control
Maintain a constant crosscheck - 90% outside, 10% inside
Know the configuration and speeds for each leg of the pattern
Ex: 95 kts, takeoff flaps, and gear on downwind. 85 kt descent on base, 75 kts, fully configured on final
Max speed in Class D airspace is 200 KIAS
Use small, controlled inputs to fly the airplane
At slow speeds, close to the ground airspeed control is very important

Controlled - The pilot receives a clearance to approach/depart and pertinent pattern information

Pattern Altitude: Usually 1,000’ AGL
A common altitude is the key factor in minimizing collisions at uncontrolled airports
The Chart Supplement will usually specify nonstandard pattern altitudes

All turns are left unless otherwise noted (Chart Supplement, Tower, Airport Markings, etc.)

Upwind Leg - The departure leg, flown parallel and in the same direction as runway heading
Crosswind Leg – The transition from the upwind leg to the downwind leg

Fly the crosswind leg to provide approximately ½ to 1-mile separation from the runway

The heading flown is opposite the landing runway

The downwind leg normally continues to a point 45o off the intended landing point, past the approach end of the runway
The turn to the base leg is started at the end of the downwind leg
Point can be adjusted based on circumstances
Wind, traffic, tower, emergency, etc.

Ground track should be perpendicular to the extended centerline
Heading is 90o off runway direction (with no wind)
Continue the descent, adjusting pitch and power to maintain airspeed, glideslope, aim point
Begin the turn to final to end up established on centerline

The base leg will be adjusted depending on wind conditions

Turn to final should be no closer than ¼ mile at an altitude appropriate for the glide slope selected

Adjust the turn from base to center the aircraft on the runway
Crab into the wind to maintain ground track
Adjust pitch and power as necessary to maintain airspeed, glideslope, and aim point
